spans.text: The Patchogu Island Prattler had been published without interruption from March 1892 to the present, which was the kind of fact the paper itself had never tired of noting. Every anniversary edition, the twenty-fifth, the fiftieth, the centennial in 1992, had led with the same claim, the same pride, the same implicit argument that continuity was itself a form of integrity. If you had been here long enough, if you had watched the island through enough seasons, you had earned a particular kind of authority that newer arrivals simply could not purchase.

The current editor was a man named Gerald Pratt, who was seventy-six and the fourth generation of Pratts to run the paper, and who understood, with the clear-eyed pride of someone who had never done anything else, that he was the living embodiment of that continuity. He had a photograph on his office wall of his great-grandfather standing at the first press, another of his grandfather beside the first electric model, and a third of his father at the desk that Gerald now occupied, which was the same desk and had been refinished twice and had coffee rings on it that predated Gerald's tenure by at least forty years.
He came into the Ginger Mae on a Tuesday morning in late July with the expression of a man who had been sitting on something uncomfortable for long enough to have grown accustomed to the discomfort.
Victoria brought his coffee. He thanked her. He turned the cup on its saucer once, which was a nervous habit she had never seen him perform before.
I need to ask you something,
he said.
All right,
she said.
About the archive.
He looked at his coffee.
The Prattler's archive. I think there may be something in it that,
He paused in the way of someone who had rehearsed this conversation and found that the rehearsal hadn't helped.
I think there may be something missing. And I think you should know about it.

Victoria called Olivia and Solei from the back room. They came out with their respective morning tasks and sat across from Gerald, who had not moved or touched his coffee, which told Victoria what she needed to know about his level of discomfort.
The archive,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei said. She said it the way she said things she had already been thinking about, which was in the tone of someone confirming a suspicion rather than hearing a new fact.
We've been meaning to look at it.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Gerald looked at her.
Why?
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: Because the Prattler covered this island for a hundred and thirty years,
she said.
And Grandma Knapp was on this island for seventy of those years. And at some point she did things that were worth covering. And we haven't found the coverage.

Gerald set down his cup. He looked at the three women with the expression of someone who had come to deliver information and had discovered that the information had already arrived by a different route.
How much do you know?
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: he said.
We know what we've found,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said.
Which is that some things are missing.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Fourteen issues,
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: Gerald said. He said it the way you said numbers you had been carrying for a long time, with relief and with something beneath the relief that was harder to name.

Fourteen issues of the Prattler are missing from the archive. Not damaged. Not lost to weather or flood or the fire in '47 that took some of the '30s issues. Missing. Removed. From 1962 to 1971, there are fourteen gaps in the archive where issues should be and aren't.
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: The kitchen was quiet.
You knew,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said.
I found it four years ago,
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: Gerald said.
When I was doing the centennial retrospective. I went through the complete run and found fourteen gaps and I,
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: He stopped.
My grandfather was the editor from 1948 to 1979. Those are his years. The missing issues are his issues.
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: And you didn't say anything,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said. She said it without accusation, because Gerald Pratt was seventy-six and had clearly been living with this for four years and the time for accusation was not right now.
I didn't know who to tell,
he said.
Or what it meant. Or whether it was better to,
He looked at his hands.
My grandfather was an honest man. I need you to understand that first. He was an honest man who covered this island for thirty years and the paper was the paper it was because of him.
And yet,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said.
And yet,
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: Gerald agreed.
Fourteen issues.
spans.speaker: Gerald

spans.text: Solei went to the archive that afternoon.

The Prattler's archive occupied the back room of the paper's building on Harbor Road, two rooms, actually, the outer one with the current files and the inner one with the bound volumes going back to 1892, the spines labeled by year in the handwriting of whoever had labeled them at the time, which meant the handwriting changed every generation and you could track the paper's history by the changing of the scripts.
Gerald had given her the key and his blessing and a look of profound relief, which was the look of a man handing off a weight he had been carrying alone.
She spent three hours in the inner room.

The room smelled of paper and cedar and the specific dry neutrality of a place that had not been opened to outside air in a long time. The bound volumes ran floor to ceiling on three walls, the spines hand-labeled in the handwriting of whoever had been maintaining the archive at the time, Solei could trace the Pratt family's history by the handwriting alone, the firm copperplate of the founding generation giving way to the rounder hand of the next and then to the compressed printing of Gerald's father and finally to the ball-point annotations of Gerald himself, who had been adding dates to the spines since he took over and who had, apparently, not wanted to disturb anything.

She found the first gap in the 1963 volume. She almost missed it, the surrounding issues were snug and the gap was narrow, the way a gap looks when something has been removed cleanly and the adjacent volumes have been settled back against each other to minimize the space. She would not have found it at all if she hadn't been running her fingertip along the spines and felt the binding give slightly, the way a file folder gives when a document has been lifted from it.
She stopped. She pulled the 1963 volume and opened it.

The staple holes were there. Two small punctures in the binding, the paper fibers around them compressed and slightly darker than the surrounding pages, the way paper looked when metal had been pressed through it repeatedly over many years. Someone had taken the issue out and replaced it and taken it out again, more than once, before the final removal.

She counted the gaps. She photographed each one. She ran her finger along the punctures and thought about a man who had been an honest journalist and had covered this island for thirty years and had, at some point, stood in this room and taken out the evidence of his own reporting.

He had not thrown it away, she suspected. That was not a decision you made lightly and then unmade. You kept what you removed. You kept it because you were not sure, and because not being sure was its own kind of keeping faith.
She noted the dates. She made a list.

The dates were: January 1963. April 1963. November 1963. March 1964. June 1965. Two in 1966, February and September. One in 1967. Three in 1968, January, June, October. And then two in 1971, March and November.
She looked at the list.
November 1963. The month she had a reason to remember.

She photographed the list. She put her notebook in her bag. She sat in the archive room for a moment with the bound volumes around her and the dust of a hundred and thirty years in the air and the particular silence of a place where information had been kept and some of it had been deliberately removed.
Then she locked the room and returned the key to Gerald and went back to the island's evening ferry.
At the kitchen table, she laid the list on the surface between the three of them.
Fourteen issues,
she said.
Victoria looked at the dates. She looked at November 1963 for a moment longer than the others.
Someone took them,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said.
Someone with access to the archive. Which over that period means Gerald's grandfather,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei paused.
Or someone Gerald's grandfather allowed access.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Why would he remove his own paper's coverage?
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said.
Because the coverage was of something he was being asked not to cover,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei said.
Or something he had covered and then decided was safer not to have covered.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: She looked at the list again.
Or something he was protecting someone from. Someone he trusted or owed.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: The kitchen was quiet. Outside, the last light was leaving the water in the way it left in late July, slowly, reluctantly, as if it had found the island worth staying for and was leaving only because it had no choice.
The Knapp family,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said.
We don't know that yet,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said.
We don't know anything yet,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei agreed.
We know the dates. We know the gaps. We know Gerald's grandfather had a reason, and the reason was important enough to him to remove the evidence.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: She closed her notebook.
We need to know what those fourteen issues covered.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: If the issues are gone,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Olivia said,
how do we find out what was in them?
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: Victoria looked at the list. At November 1963.
We find the people who were there,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: she said.
